messages.subject_clean: Serialized plot objects are very big
messages.body_plain:
I am creating a series of trellis plots in a map/reduce job.  I
serialize them using rhcollect(key, serialize(p, NULL) where p is the
plot object.

What is strange is that of these serialized objects should be quite
small.  When I perform the operation with one key/value pair in my
local session, The serialized object is about 0.1 MB.  However, each
individual plot I get back when I rhread the entire map/reduce results
is 6 MB.  Does anyone know why the Rhipe job would save a much larger
serialized plot object than what I get in a local session?

Here's an example:
I create a plot "pp" in my local session, using data read from the
hdfs through rhgetkey (trying to replicate what would be seen in a map/
reduce as much as possible)

> length(serialize(pp, NULL))
12971

However, when I read in a serialized plot object from my map/reduce
job for the corresponding key,
> length(serialized_object_from_rhipe_job)
7065237

But when I deserialize the one read from Rhipe, the size is
comparable:

> object.size(pp)
83224 bytes
> object.size(serialized_object_from_rhipe_job)
79016 bytes

It's a little troublesome that they're not the same, although both
plots look the same when printed.

Any ideas on why this is happening?  I need my plot objects to be
small.

messages.body_plain:
The issue seems to be somewhere between when the data is serialized to
protocol buffers and written to disk.  When I use rhsz, things look
fine.

Since I can't replicate my real-world example, here's a dummy example
that kind of illustrates the issue:

# dummy set of data - keys are letters a-z, values are random normal
vectors, length 10000
N <- 10000
set.seed(12345)
d <- data.frame(let=sample(letters, N, replace=TRUE), dat=rnorm(N))

d1 <- lapply(seq_along(letters), function(ii) {
   list(k=letters[ii], v=subset(d, let==letters[ii])$dat)
})

rhwrite(d1, "tmpdat")

setup <- expression({
   library(lattice)
})

map <- expression({
   lapply(seq_along(map.values), function(r) {
      k <- map.keys[[r]]
      v <- map.values[[r]]

      val <- NULL
      pp <- histogram(v)
      rhcollect(k, serialize(pp, NULL))
   })
})

z <- rhmr(setup=setup, map=map,
   ifolder="tmpdat",
   ofolder="tmpdat_histogram",
   inout=c("sequence", "sequence"),
   mapred=list(mapred.reduce.tasks=0)
)

rhex(z)

# for key 'a'
# make the same plot on our local machine (will be a little different
internally because data source has a different name)
pp <- histogram(d1[[1]][[2]])

# read in result
res <- rhread("tmpdat_histogram/p*")

# this is a list - for each element:
# - first element is the key, a-z
# - second element is the serialized plot (already 'rhuz'-ed from
rhread), so it is just serialized in R binary format

# compare the size of the actual plot object read in from our map-
reduce job (need to unserialize) and the local one
object.size(pp)
# 77392 bytes
object.size(unserialize(res[[1]][[2]]))
# 77216 bytes
# about the same size

# compare the R binary format size for the local and the one read in
from our map-reduce job:
object.size(serialize(pp, NULL))
# 29312 bytes
object.size(res[[1]][[2]])
# 44392 bytes

# result read in from Rhipe is 1.5x larger

This is what I'm experiencing with my real application, except that
the difference in size is >500x

BTW is there a reason for the creation of a new file with a random
name other then the seding?  If not try this as your mscript.sh.  IMO
this is clearer and also doesn't depend on a sed statement that has to
be different for everyone.

The gist of the following script snippet is create all the
environmental variables that R does, set LD_LIBRARY_PATH, and jump
straight to the lines that R CMD invokes in the R script.  Avoids
having to create new files.

##################### Works for me as mscript.sh
##################################

bin=`dirname "$0"`
RHIPE_HOME=`cd "$bin"; pwd`
export R_HOME=$RHIPE_HOME/R
export R_HOME_DIR=$R_HOME
export R_SHARE_DIR=$R_HOME/share
export R_INCLUDE_DIR=$R_HOME/include
export R_DOC_DIR=$R_HOME/doc
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$R_HOME/lib:$RHIPE_HOME
chmod -R 777 $RHIPE_HOME
. "${R_HOME}/etc${R_ARCH}/ldpaths"
exec sh $R_HOME/bin/Rcmd $RHIPE_HOME/imperious.so --slave --silent --
vanilla

#################### end mscript.sh
############################################

system commands.  There is no sensible default for hdfs.tar.filename
so I left it without one, but what you use for a runner command
depends on that archive filename. See examples.  Tested on two
clusters with a bash shell.  Testing on non-bash shells isn't in my

# createRhipeLibArchive
#' THIS ONLY IS EXPECTED TO WORK FOR SOMEONE USING A BASH SHELL.  IT
IS UNTESTED ON OTHER SHELLS.
#' Create an archive on the HDFS with everything need to run Rhipe in
MapReduce task.  Code has been borrowed from Saptarshi Guha.
#' Note as a side effect it reloads the library (necessary).  This
means if you called rhoptions to set anything you will have to call it
again.
#' Recommend you "rm -Rf" on local.tmp.dir if it exist before
calling.  I did not in case the user wants to create it ahead of time
and put other stuff to be archived into it.
#' Pay particular attention to the hdfs.tar.filename option.  It does
not have a default because there is no sensible default location that
won't error for most users.
#'
#' @param local.tmp.dir The directory to use prior to tar zipping the
archive.  This is deleted if delete.local.tmp.dir == TRUE.
#' @param local.tar.file The file to create on the local file system.
Must have a path! If you do not have a path on the filename this
function will fail due to the use of "tar". This is not deleted.
#' @param hdfs.tar.file The filename on the hdfs of the created
archive.  This should have a path to the file in addition to the
archive name.
#' @param delete.local.tmp.dir Delete the local.tmp.dir before
returning if TRUE.
#' @param rhipe.runner.file Filename to copy as a runner script. If
this is NULL a default runner is used that should work for most
people.  If the default runner is used then if hdfs.tar.filename is
"filename.tar.gz" the appropriate runner option for rhipe is
rhoption(runner="sh ./filename/rhipe.C.sh <http://rhipe.C.sh>"). See examples.
#' @author Jeremiah Rounds \email{roundsj...@gmail.com}
#'
#' @examples
#'
#' ##### Two different runners depending on the hdfs.tar.filename
argument #####
#'
#' ##### Example 1 ######
#' system("rm -Rf ~/Rdist")
#' createRhipeLibArchive("~/Rdist", "~/Rfolder.tar.gz", "/
Rfolder.tar.gz",delete.local.tmp.dir=FALSE)
#' rhoptions(runner = "sh ./Rfolder/rhipe.C.sh <http://rhipe.C.sh>")
#' ##### Example 2 ######
#' system("rm -Rf ~/RhipeLib")
#' createRhipeLibArchive(hdfs.tar.filename="/wsc/jrounds/
RhipeLib.tar.gz",delete.local.tmp.dir=FALSE)
#' rhoptions(runner="sh ./RhipeLib/rhipe.C.sh <http://rhipe.C.sh>")

createRhipeLibArchive = function(local.tmp.dir="~/RhipeLib",
local.tar.filename="~/RhipeLib.tar.gz", hdfs.tar.filename,
delete.local.tmp.dir=TRUE, rhipe.runner.file=NULL){
    #HELPER FUCTIONS

    #The built in R file copy routine had issues for me.
    file.copy = function(src,dest,...){
        system(paste("cp -RH",src,dest))
    }
    createRhipeRunner = function(filename){
        exprToLines = function(expr){
            lines = deparse(expr)
            lines = lines[-1]
            lines = lines[-length(lines)]
            return(lines)
        }
        file = file(filename,"w")
        cat(
'bin=`dirname "$0"`
RHIPE_HOME=`cd "$bin"; pwd`
export R_HOME=$RHIPE_HOME/R
export R_HOME_DIR=$R_HOME
export R_SHARE_DIR=$R_HOME/share
export R_INCLUDE_DIR=$R_HOME/include
export R_DOC_DIR=$R_HOME/doc
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$R_HOME/lib:$RHIPE_HOME
chmod -R 777 $RHIPE_HOME
. "${R_HOME}/etc${R_ARCH}/ldpaths"
exec sh $R_HOME/bin/Rcmd $RHIPE_HOME/imperious.so --slave --silent --
vanilla
'           ,
            file=file
        )
        close(file)

    }

    #can't have values in runner that don't make sense in the archive
creation
    try({detach("package:Rhipe")},silent=TRUE)
    try({unloadNamespace("Rhipe")},silent=TRUE)
    library(Rhipe)
    rhinit()

    # BEGIN THE WORK OF ARCHIVE CREATION

    tfolder <- local.tmp.dir
    dir.create(tfolder)

    # Fill the temp directory with everything Rhipe needs
    a <- system(sprintf("ldd  %s",rhoptions()[[3]][1]),intern=TRUE)
    b <- lapply(strsplit(a,"=>"), function(r) if (length(r)>=2) r[2]
else NULL)
    b <- strsplit(unlist(b)," ")
    b <- unlist(lapply(b,"[[",2))
    b <-unlist( sapply(b, function(r) if(nchar(r)>1) r else NULL))
    for(x in b) file.copy(x,tfolder) ##copies the linked .so files
    file.copy(rhoptions()[[3]][1],tfolder)  ## copies the RHIPE C
engine
    file.copy(R.home(),tfolder)
    ## R_LIBS
    x <- Sys.getenv("R_LIBS")
    if(nchar(x)>1){
        for(y in list.files(x,full.names=TRUE))
file.copy(y,sprintf("%s/R/library/",tfolder), recursive=TRUE)
    }

    #Deal with the runner.
    if(!is.null(rhipe.runner.file))
        file.copy(rhipe.runner.file,tfolder)
    else
        createRhipeRunner(paste(tfolder,"rhipe.C.sh <http://rhipe.C.sh>",sep="/"))

    #build the archive

    system(paste("cd", local.tmp.dir,";tar cvfz",
local.tar.filename,"*"))
    rhput(local.tar.filename,hdfs.tar.filename)
    if(delete.local.tmp.dir)
        system(paste("rm -R", local.tmp.dir))
}

createRhipeLibArchive(hdfs.tar.filename="/wsc/jrounds/
RhipeLib.tar.gz",delete.local.tmp.dir=FALSE)
rhoptions(runner="sh ./RhipeLib/rhipe.C.sh <http://rhipe.C.sh>")

messages.subject: Never append in the reduce$reduce
messages.body_plain:
This message is about effficient use of Rhipe.

It has seemed inevitable in data analysis that we eventually need to
collect all the Key,Value pairs for a key in the reduce with reduce.

Typically this looks something like
reduce = expression(
  pre = { data = list()},
  reduce = { data = append(data,reduce.values)},
  post = { data = do.call("rbind",data); #work here#}
)

I basically inherited this paradigm from looking at code of people
that came before me, but it can be improved and just in case it has
been adopted  by other people I remark about it today. Append is known
to be slow at big n, but what to do about it didn't occur to me until
Friday.  Turns out it is easy to make a list of list and manipulate
that for huge time savings.

A co-worker of mine was parsing 5 million line text files in MapReduce
and one file was running at like 6 minutes and one file was running at
60 minutes, and he said, "Why if they are both 5 million lines?" to
me.  I took a look at it, discovered the long one was kicking out 4
million lines to one key.  I then thought why is that slow?  Turned
out it was not the shuffle: these were 1 gb files.  Eventually I
tracked it down to the reduce append via counters, and that would be
the end of the story if I had not realized there is a logically
equivalent operation that runs so much faster in R.  Apply the changes
represented below changed a 60 minute job into a 7 minute job.

reduce = expression(
  pre = { data = list()},
  reduce = { data[[length(data) + 1]] = reduce.values}
  post = { data = do.call("rbind", unlist(data,recursive=FALSE));
#work here#}
)

As a stand alone example of the change to list of list timing consider
this snippet:

buffer = lapply(1:10000,function(i) runif(10))
mock.reduce.and.post.v1 = function(){
	data = list()
	for(i in 1:125){
		data = append(data,buffer)
	}
	data = do.call("rbind",data)
	print(summary(data))
	return()
}
mock.reduce.and.post.v2 = function(){
	data = list()
	for(i in 1:125){
		n = length(data)
		data[[n+1]] = buffer
	}
	data = unlist(data,recursive =FALSE)
	data = do.call("rbind",data)
	print(summary(data))
	return()
}
#this is 71 seconds on my system
system.time({mock.reduce.and.post.v1()})
#this is 19.5 seconds on my system
system.time({mock.reduce.and.post.v2()})

That 3 times faster advantage only gets more extreme as the inner loop
increases in size.     I am not sure the rate of growth I would have
to plot it at different n.  You don't entirely avoid the issue of poor
inserts in R, but since the list is grow at 1 per a loop instead of
10000 per a loop you put off the inevitable annoying slow insert long
enough for a MapReduce of even fairly extreme amount of values for one
Key to finish in a timely fashion.

BTW this parsing log files into data structures is a good reason to
allow buffer sizes of greater then 10k K/V in Rhipe isn't it?
